title: Decimal place value: reading and comparing decimals
subject: MATH

authority.note: Curriculum V2 draft. Requires exact-revision human review; not approved, not published.

objectives.statement: Name the place and value of any digit in a decimal number up to thousandths.
Compare and order decimals up to thousandths by comparing place by place, and explain the comparison.

scenes.title: Which bag of rice is heavier?

content.body:
At the market, Musu weighs two small bags of rice. One scale shows **1.5 kg**. The other shows **1.25 kg**.

Her brother says the second bag is heavier because 25 is bigger than 5. Is he right? By the end of this lesson you will know, and you will be able to explain why.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two scale readings, 1.5 kg and 1.25 kg, and the question of which bag of rice is heavier.

offline.fallback: Text only; saved with the lesson.

content.body:
Today you will learn to:

1. Name the place and value of any digit in a decimal, up to thousandths.
2. Compare and order decimals by checking place by place, and explain which is larger.

At the end you will show both on your own, without help.

accessibility.textAlternative: The two lesson goals: naming the place and value of decimal digits, and comparing decimals place by place.

content.body: Two quick questions about ideas we will build on. If either one is hard, tell your teacher: you will get a short review first.

content.body:
The decimal point separates whole ones from parts of a one. Places after the point are **tenths**, **hundredths** and **thousandths**. Each place is worth one tenth of the place to its left.

In **3.472**: the 3 is 3 ones (3), the 4 is 4 tenths (0.4), the 7 is 7 hundredths (0.07) and the 2 is 2 thousandths (0.002).
keyPoints: There is no 'oneths' place: the first place after the point is tenths.
Read 3.472 as three and four hundred seventy-two thousandths.

content.body: The number 15.258 has two 5s. They are worth very different amounts because they sit in different places. Reveal one step at a time.

steps.label: Find the point
steps.description: Everything left of the point is whole ones and tens: 15. Everything right of it is parts: .258.

steps.label: Whole part
steps.description: The 1 is 1 ten (10). The first 5 is 5 ones (5).

steps.label: First place after the point
steps.description: The 2 is in the tenths place: 2 tenths, 0.2.

steps.label: Second place
steps.description: The second 5 is in the hundredths place: 5 hundredths, 0.05.

steps.label: Third place
steps.description: The 8 is in the thousandths place: 8 thousandths, 0.008.

accessibility.textAlternative: Six revealed steps naming the value of each digit of 15.258: 10, 5, 0.2, 0.05 and 0.008.

offline.fallback: Steps are saved with the lesson.

content.body: A zero after the point keeps a place empty, so the digits after it move one place to the right. Use the chart for these two.

feedback.correct: Yes. The 0 holds the tenths place, so the 7 is in the hundredths place.
feedback.incorrect: The 0 fills the tenths place, so the 7 is pushed into the hundredths place.

optionFeedback: The 0 fills the tenths place, so the 7 is pushed into the hundredths place.
Yes. The 0 holds the tenths place, so the 7 is in the hundredths place.
The 7 is to the right of the point, so it is part of a one.

feedback.correct: Yes. Zero tenths, then 5 in the hundredths place.
feedback.incorrect: 0.5 is five tenths. Hundredths need a second place after the point.

optionFeedback: 0.5 is five tenths. Hundredths need a second place after the point.
0.005 is five thousandths: the 5 is three places after the point.
Yes. Zero tenths, then 5 in the hundredths place.

content.body: To compare decimals, line up the points and compare place by place from the left. The first place that differs decides.

steps.label: Line up the points
steps.description: Write 1.5 above 1.25 so the points are in one column.

steps.label: Fill empty places
steps.description: Write 1.5 as 1.50. Adding a zero at the end does not change the value.

steps.label: Compare ones
steps.description: Both have 1 one. Same, so move right.

steps.label: Decide
steps.description: 1.5 > 1.25. The 1.5 kg bag is heavier. Having more digits did not make 1.25 larger.

accessibility.textAlternative: Five revealed steps comparing 1.50 and 1.25 by lining up the points and comparing ones, then tenths.

offline.fallback: Steps are saved with the lesson.

content.body: Line up the points and give both numbers the same number of places before you compare.

feedback.correct: Yes. 0.40 and 0.45 have the same tenths, and 5 hundredths > 0 hundredths.
feedback.incorrect: Write 0.4 as 0.40. Same tenths; then 5 hundredths beats 0 hundredths.

Yes. 0.40 and 0.45 have the same tenths, and 5 hundredths > 0 hundredths.
They share 4 tenths, but 0.45 also has 5 hundredths.

feedback.correct: Yes. 0.5 has 5 tenths; 0.125 has only 1 tenth.
feedback.incorrect: 125 > 5 for whole numbers, but compare tenths here: 1 tenth against 5 tenths.

optionFeedback: 125 > 5 for whole numbers, but compare tenths here: 1 tenth against 5 tenths.
Yes. 0.5 has 5 tenths; 0.125 has only 1 tenth.

content.body: Kollie says 2.35 is larger than 2.4 because 35 is more than 4. Sia says 2.4 is larger because it has more tenths. Who is right?

feedback.correct: Yes. Both have 2 ones; 4 tenths > 3 tenths, so 2.4 > 2.35.
feedback.incorrect: 35 and 4 are not whole numbers here. Compare tenths: 2.35 has 3 tenths, 2.4 has 4 tenths.

optionFeedback: 35 and 4 are not whole numbers here. Compare tenths: 2.35 has 3 tenths, 2.4 has 4 tenths.
Yes. Both have 2 ones; 4 tenths > 3 tenths, so 2.4 > 2.35.

content.body:
Go back to Musu's rice: which bag was heavier, and how do you know? Say your reason to a partner.

In one week your teacher will ask a few questions like today's again, without notes. That helps the idea stay with you. Next lesson, you will use place value to round decimals.
